q: How much chiller energy does raising the chilled water temperature by 1 degree save?
title: Chiller saving per degree of chilled water
short: About 3% of chiller compressor power for each 1 degree C you raise the evaporator temperature, according to BEE's guide book on electrical utilities. Raising chilled water supply from 7 to 9 degrees C on a busy process chiller can cut its electricity by around 6%, provided the process still gets the cooling it needs.
audience: Plant engineers in pharma, food, plastics and commercial buildings

sections.h: Why a warmer setpoint saves power
p: A chiller's compressor works to lift heat from the evaporator pressure up to the condenser pressure. A warmer chilled water setpoint raises the evaporator temperature and pressure, so the lift is smaller and the compressor does less work for the same cooling. The 3% per degree figure is a rule of thumb for vapour compression chillers; your machine's part-load data sheet gives a closer number.

sections.h: How far you can raise it
ul: Check the coldest user first: a jacketed reactor, a mould, a cold room or an air handler that must remove moisture.
Air handlers that dehumidify need cold enough water to bring coil temperature below the dew point; raising the setpoint too far raises room humidity.
Watch pump energy: warmer water carries less cooling per litre at the same temperature difference, so flow may rise and pumps work harder.
Raise in steps of 0.5 to 1 degree, and log product quality and room conditions for a week at each step.

sections.h: Turning the saving into kWh and CO2
ol: Find the chiller's annual kWh: from a submeter, or kW per TR times TR times running hours.
Multiply by 3% per degree raised to get kWh saved.
Multiply kWh saved by the grid factor, 0.710 kg CO2 per kWh for FY 2024-25, for location-based Scope 2.
Compare the next year's chiller kWh at similar load and weather to confirm the saving.

p: Applying 3% to the whole plant's electricity instead of the chiller alone; counting the saving at full load when the chiller runs mostly at part load; and raising the setpoint while users open their valves fully to compensate, which wipes out the gain.

example.title: Worked example: a 200 TR process chiller
lines: Running: 200 TR x 0.8 kW per TR = 160 kW, for 6,000 hours a year
Setpoint raised by 2 degrees C: about 3% x 2 = 6% saved
CO2 saved: 57,600 x 0.710 = 40,896 kg, about 40.9 t CO2 a year
example.note: The 3% per degree is BEE's rule of thumb; confirm with before and after submeter readings.

senseible: Senseible reads kWh from your electricity bills and converts kWh to CO2 at the CEA factor of 0.710 kg CO2 per kWh for FY 2024-25, so a lower chiller load shows up in your monthly Scope 2 records.
